paras: The attempted expulsion of W. M. Grayor from Paducah was a failed effort on the night of July 8, 1903, by a group of Paducah residents to escort Grayor, a Black street preacher, out of the Kentucky city and warn him not to return. The group acted the day a special judge fined Grayor for speeches said to incite race trouble, but could not find him. The episode is known only from a single report in the Paducah Sun, which attributed it to unnamed "reports."

Grayor, styled "Rev." by the Sun with the title in quotation marks, preached on Paducah street corners to followers the paper called the "Do Right" people. He had earlier been fined $50 in police court for immorality and had appealed that judgment to the circuit court. On Saturday night, July 4, Officers Clark, Johnson and Woods arrested him for language in his public addresses "tending to incite riot," and the case was continued when he appeared before Judge Sanders on July 6.

Special Judge Tom Crice heard the charge of using improper language in street sermons on the afternoon of July 7 and reserved his decision. The hearing drew notice when patrol wagon driver John Austin took offense at a remark by Grayor's attorney, J. Wheeler Campbell, and wanted to fight him after court, though the two later made up. Late on July 8 Crice fined Grayor $15 and costs, about $30 in all, which Grayor paid.

That night, according to the Sun, "a number of people who think that Grayor is a hypocite and trouble-breeder" went out to escort him from the city and advise him to stay away, but he could not be found. The paper did not name the members of the party or give their number. It reported Grayor still in the city "so far as is known" the next day.

The police told the Sun they did not believe Grayor would "take any chances by remaining here," and no action against the search party appears in the coverage. In August the Indianapolis Freeman's Cairo, Illinois, correspondent reported that Rev. Grayor of Paducah had preached two sermons in Cairo and left for Washington, D.C., to speak. He was back in Paducah courts in September 1904, when a circuit-court jury acquitted him on appeal of the earlier immorality charge without leaving its seat.

The Paducah Sun covered Grayor's case in its city hall and police-court columns over four days, and the search party appeared as a subheading, "Searching Party Went Out, But Could Not Find Him," above routine items on dog licenses and stray cows. The paper allowed that "there is no objection to free speech," but said his language was "said to have a tendency to incite race trouble" and reported "a disposition in some quarters to make him 'move on'" without criticizing the attempt. No other white paper is known to have carried the story.

The Black press did not report the attempted expulsion. Its only mention of Grayor that summer, in the Freeman's Cairo column, presented him as a traveling preacher and "an excellent speaker" and said nothing of his trouble in Paducah.

reader.title: Attempted expulsion of W. M. Grayor from Paducah
bases: A party set out at night to escort Grayor out of Paducah and tell him to stay away, an attempted expulsion of one man that failed because he could not be found (A5).
The search party is reported only by the Paducah Sun, which itself attributes it to 'reports' (A5); the arrest and fine are documented in the same paper's police-court columns (A2, A4, A5).

accounts.label: Paducah Sun police-court reporting
accounts.gist: Grayor was arrested for speeches said to incite riot, tried before a special judge and fined; 'according to reports' a party then went out to escort him from the city but could not find him.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Cairo)
accounts.gist: Rev. Grayor of Paducah preached two sermons in Cairo and left for Washington, D.C.; called 'an excellent speaker'; no mention of the arrest or the search party.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'Searching Party Went Out, But Could Not Find Him,' allowed that 'there is no objection to free speech' but repeated the party's view of him as a 'trouble-breeder' and voiced no criticism of the attempt to drive him out.
The Freeman's Cairo column treated Grayor as a visiting preacher and 'excellent speaker' and said nothing of the Paducah trouble.

"Rev." W. M. (William) Grayor, a "colored" street preacher called the "Do Right" preacher

Unnamed 'number of people who think that Grayor is a hypocite and trouble-breeder'; race not stated
Fined $15 and costs (about $30 in all), which he paid; reported still in the city after the search
